title: Stewart v. Rosenblum
description: Whether sections 110-6 and 110-6.1 of the Pretrial Fairness Act violate the separation of powers clause of the Illinois Constitution by unduly infringing on a circuit court judge's inherent authority to detain defendants indefinitely pending trial.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioner, Aimee Stewart, argued that her indefinite detention was unlawful because the Pretrial Fairness Act did not provide statutory authority for it, and the judge's declaration of the Act as unconstitutional was premature and incorrect.
defendant_argument: The respondent, Judge Steven J. Rosenblum, argued that the Pretrial Fairness Act was unconstitutional as applied to the petitioner's case because it unduly limited his inherent judicial authority to administer justice and manage his docket, especially when a defendant repeatedly fails to appear in court.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's judgment, finding that the Pretrial Fairness Act is constitutional and does not violate the separation of powers clause, and that the respondent lacked the authority to indefinitely detain the petitioner. The court granted the petitioner's writ of habeas corpus and ordered her immediate release.

title: State v. Spencer
description: Whether Eugene Spencer's 100-year aggregate sentence, with eligibility for parole after 20 years, constitutes a de facto life sentence that violates the Illinois proportionate penalties clause for an emerging adult.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Spencer's 100-year sentence is not a de facto life sentence because he is eligible for parole after serving 20 years, and the youth parole statute (730 ILCS 5/5-4.5-115(b)) provides a meaningful opportunity for release.
defendant_argument: Spencer argued that his 100-year sentence is a de facto life sentence that violates the Illinois proportionate penalties clause because it was imposed without sufficient consideration of youth-related factors, and the parole statute does not provide a meaningful opportunity for parole.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's judgment that Spencer's sentence is not a de facto life sentence, but clarified that he is not precluded from bringing an as-applied challenge to his sentence under the proportionate penalties clause in a postconviction proceeding.

title: McCombie v. Illinois State Board of Elections
description: Whether the plaintiffs' motion to challenge the 2021 legislative redistricting plan, alleging violations of constitutional requirements for compact districts and partisan gerrymandering, is timely or barred by the equitable doctrine of laches.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue their motion to challenge the 2021 Enacted Plan is timely and that the plan violates the Illinois Constitution's requirements for compact, contiguous, and substantially equal legislative districts, as well as political fairness by engaging in partisan gerrymandering.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the plaintiffs' motion is untimely and barred by the equitable doctrine of laches, as it was filed more than three years and two election cycles after the redistricting map was enacted.
decision_outcome: The court denied the plaintiffs' motion for leave to file a complaint for declaratory judgment and injunctive relief, ruling that it was untimely and barred by the doctrine of laches.

title: People v. Hagestedt
description: Whether police officers' actions of using a flashlight and an angled view to peer into a chained and locked, slightly ajar kitchen cabinet during a gas leak investigation constituted an unreasonable warrantless search in violation of the Fourth Amendment.
plaintiff_argument: The police officers exceeded the scope of their authorized entry (gas leak investigation) and conducted an unreasonable warrantless search by using a flashlight to peer into a chained and locked cabinet, whose contents were not in plain view, thereby violating his Fourth Amendment rights.
defendant_argument: The officers' actions did not constitute a search because the contents were openly or plainly visible, and the use of a flashlight to illuminate a darkened area does not transform an observation into a search. The defendant also failed to prove a reasonable expectation of privacy.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower courts' judgments, ruling that the trial court erred in denying the defendant's motion to suppress evidence, and vacated the defendant's conviction and sentence.

title: People v. White
description: Whether Sedrick White's 40-year sentence for first-degree murder, imposed when he was 20 years old, violates the proportionate penalties clause of the Illinois Constitution and the Eighth Amendment, given his youth and rehabilitative potential.
plaintiff_argument: Sedrick White argued that his 40-year sentence constituted a de facto life sentence, violating constitutional protections due to the court's failure to adequately consider his youth and rehabilitative potential, and that his blind guilty plea did not waive this challenge.
defendant_argument: The State argued that White's 40-year sentence was proportionate to the offense and did not shock the moral sense of the community, and that the circuit court properly considered all relevant factors, including his age, conceding that an open guilty plea does not waive sentencing errors.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's judgment, finding that Sedrick White's 40-year sentence for first-degree murder did not violate the proportionate penalties clause of the Illinois Constitution.

title: Martin v. Goodrich Corporation
description: Whether section 1(f) of the Workers' Occupational Diseases Act is a statute of repose, and if so, whether the exception in section 1.1 applies prospectively without violating Illinois's due process guarantee, with the plaintiff arguing for its application to allow a civil suit and the defendant arguing against it to maintain exclusivity provisions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that section 1(f) is a statute of repose, and the exception in section 1.1 should apply to her case, allowing her to pursue a civil action for her husband's occupational disease and death.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that section 1(f) is not a statute of repose, thus section 1.1 does not apply, and alternatively, that applying section 1.1 to revive the plaintiff's claim would violate their due process rights by infringing on a vested right to a defense.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that section 1(f) is a statute of repose, section 1.1 applies prospectively under section 4 of the Statute on Statutes, and this prospective application does not violate Illinois's due process guarantee, thereby allowing claims like the plaintiff's to proceed.

title: People v. Clark
description: Whether warrantless arrests based on investigative alerts violate the Illinois Constitution and whether the sentencing court properly considered factors for juvenile offenders.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that warrantless arrests based on probable cause, even via investigative alerts, are constitutional under both federal and state law, and that the sentencing court adequately considered factors for juvenile offenders.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that his warrantless arrest based on an investigative alert violated the Fourth Amendment and the Illinois Constitution, and that the sentencing court failed to properly consider statutory mitigating factors for juvenile offenders.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's judgment, upholding the defendant's convictions and sentence.

title: Walker v. Chasteen
description: Whether the circuit court has subject-matter jurisdiction to order refunds of unconstitutional mortgage foreclosure filing fees, or if such claims are barred by sovereign immunity and must be brought in the Court of Claims.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the officer-suit exception to sovereign immunity applies to both prospective injunctive relief and claims for refunds of unconstitutional fees, making the refund claim inextricably tied to the injunction and within the circuit court's jurisdiction, seeking restitution rather than damages.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the officer-suit exception only applied to prospective injunctive relief, and once the unconstitutional statutes were enjoined, the exception ceased to apply to the refund claim, which is a present claim against the State for a past wrong and thus falls under sovereign immunity, requiring it to be heard in the Court of Claims.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the appellate court's judgment, holding that the circuit court lacked jurisdiction over the refund claim due to sovereign immunity, and affirmed the circuit court's dismissal, meaning the claim must be brought in the Court of Claims.

title: Arlington Heights Pension Fund v. Pritzker
description: Whether Public Act 101-610, which consolidated local police and firefighter pension fund assets into statewide funds, violates the pension protection clause or the takings clause of the Illinois Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Act diminishes and impairs pension benefits by diluting voting power, affecting investment control, imposing transition costs, and constitutes a taking of private property by requiring the transfer of fund assets and bearing associated costs.
defendant_argument: The Act does not violate the pension protection clause because it does not affect the value of monetary pension benefits, and the takings clause is inapplicable as it concerns real property, not the management of fund assets.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's judgment, which upheld the circuit court's decision to grant summary judgment in favor of the defendants, finding that the Act did not violate the pension protection clause or the takings clause.

title: Caulkins v. Pritzker
description: Whether the exemptions in the Protect Illinois Communities Act, which restrict certain firearms and related items, violate the equal protection and special legislation clauses of the Illinois Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Act's exemptions for trained professionals and grandfathered individuals violate the equal protection and special legislation clauses of the Illinois Constitution, and that the Act also violated the three-readings requirement.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the exemptions do not violate equal protection or special legislation because the plaintiffs are not similarly situated to the exempt classes, and that the three-readings claim was procedurally barred.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's judgment, ruling that the Act's exemptions do not violate equal protection or special legislation, and found the plaintiffs' other claims were waived or procedurally barred.

title: Rowe v. Raoul
description: Whether Public Acts 101-652 and 102-1104 (SAFE-T Act), which abolished monetary bail and revised pretrial release provisions, violate the Illinois Constitution's bail clause, crime victims' rights clause, and separation of powers clause.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Act's pretrial release provisions violated the Illinois Constitution's bail clause, crime victims' rights clause, and separation of powers clause, contending that eliminating monetary bail was an improper constitutional amendment, stripped courts of authority, and prevented the protection of victims' safety.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Act was constitutional, asserting that the bail clause does not mandate monetary bail, the Act's provisions adequately consider crime victims' rights, and the legislature has the authority to regulate the bail system without violating separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's decision, ruling that the Public Acts 101-652 and 102-1104 (SAFE-T Act) are constitutional and do not violate the Illinois Constitution.

title: People v. Mayfield
description: Whether the Illinois Supreme Court's emergency administrative orders, which tolled the speedy-trial statute during the COVID-19 pandemic, violated the Illinois Constitution's separation-of-powers clause by infringing on the General Assembly's legislative authority.
plaintiff_argument: The court's administrative orders were a valid exercise of its constitutional authority over court procedure and did not violate the separation-of-powers clause, thus the defendant's conviction should be affirmed.
defendant_argument: The court's administrative orders unconstitutionally infringed on the legislature's authority by suspending the speedy-trial statute, compelling reversal of his conviction.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the defendant's conviction, holding that its emergency orders tolling the speedy-trial statute did not violate the separation-of-powers clause.

title: People v. Brown
description: Whether defendant Servetus Brown received ineffective assistance of trial counsel because his attorney agreed to a process where juror challenges were exercised off the record and outside his presence, thereby violating his constitutional right to be present at a critical stage of trial.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the defendant's counsel provided adequate assistance and that the defendant failed to demonstrate prejudice from the jury selection process.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that his trial counsel was ineffective for failing to object to the off-the-record sidebar conferences for juror challenges, which violated his constitutional right to be present during a critical stage of trial.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the appellate court, which had affirmed the circuit court's judgment, thereby upholding the defendant's conviction.

title: Illinois Road & Transportation Builders Association v. The County of Cook
description: Whether the 2016 'safe roads amendment' to the Illinois Constitution, which mandates that transportation-related revenues be used only for transportation purposes, applies to revenues generated by home-rule units from transportation-related taxes, with the plaintiff arguing it does and the defendant arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The Amendment applies to all moneys derived from transportation-related taxes, fees, excises, or license taxes, including those collected by home-rule units like Cook County, and thus the County is impermissibly diverting these funds for non-transportation purposes.
defendant_argument: The Amendment applies exclusively to state-imposed tax revenues, not revenues imposed by home-rule authority, and therefore Cook County's spending of transportation-related tax revenues on public safety operations is permissible under its home-rule powers.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's dismissal of the plaintiffs' complaint, finding that the plaintiffs have associational standing and that the Cook County Transportation Taxes are subject to the Amendment, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: People v. Moon
description: Whether a criminal defendant's trial before an unsworn jury requires automatic reversal without a showing of prejudice to the defendant, with the defendant arguing for automatic reversal and the plaintiff arguing against it without a showing of prejudice.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the defendant forfeited the error by not objecting at trial, and even if it was an error, it was harmless and did not constitute plain error requiring automatic reversal without a showing of prejudice.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the circuit court's failure to administer a trial oath to the jury was a "clear error" and a structural error, requiring automatic reversal regardless of the strength of the evidence or any showing of prejudice.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the appellate and circuit courts' judgments, the defendant's conviction and sentence, and remanded the case for a new trial, concluding that the complete failure to swear the jury with a trial oath was structural error.

title: International Association of Fire Fighters, Local 50 v. The City of Peoria
description: Whether the City of Peoria, as a home rule unit, can define "catastrophic injury" and "injury" in its local ordinance in a manner inconsistent with the state's Public Safety Employee Benefits Act and prior Illinois Supreme Court interpretations.
plaintiff_argument: The Union argued that the City's ordinance improperly redefined "catastrophic injury" and "injury" in a way that violates the Public Safety Employee Benefits Act and established case law, exceeding its home rule authority.
defendant_argument: The City argued it had home rule authority to define these terms for itself, was not bound by prior judicial interpretations without legislative amendment, and that its ordinance was a proper exercise of its powers.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the lower courts' decisions, ruling that the City's ordinance definitions of "catastrophic injury," "injury," and "gainful work" were inconsistent with the Public Safety Employee Benefits Act and therefore invalid.

title: People v. House
description: Whether Antonio House's mandatory natural life sentence for murders committed at age 19 violates the proportionate penalties clause of the Illinois Constitution, and whether his actual innocence claim warrants further review.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the appellate court erroneously considered the as-applied proportionate penalties claim without a sufficiently developed evidentiary record, and that the mandatory life sentence for an adult offender is constitutional. They also agreed to remand the actual innocence claim for reconsideration in light of new precedent.
defendant_argument: House argued that his mandatory natural life sentence was unconstitutional as applied to him under the proportionate penalties clause, citing evolving science on juvenile maturity and brain development that should extend Miller v. Alabama protections to young adults aged 18-21. He also argued for cross-relief on his actual innocence claim based on newly discovered evidence.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the appellate court's finding that the petitioner's sentence violated the proportionate penalties clause and vacated the appellate court's judgment affirming the dismissal of the petitioner's actual innocence claim, remanding the entire cause to the circuit court for further second-stage postconviction proceedings on both issues.

title: People v. McCavitt
description: Whether the police violated the Fourth Amendment by searching the defendant's computer for child pornography after his acquittal on sexual assault charges, using data previously seized under a warrant that also covered unauthorized video recording, without obtaining a new warrant.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the search for child pornography was lawful because the original warrant authorized a search for unauthorized video recording, which was not resolved by the sexual assault acquittal, and the child pornography was discovered in plain view during a search reasonably directed at that authorized purpose.
defendant_argument: McCavitt argued that his acquittal for sexual assault restored his expectation of privacy in his computer data, making any subsequent search without a new warrant unlawful and a violation of his Fourth Amendment rights, especially given the delay in the search.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the appellate court's judgment, affirming the trial court's denial of the defendant's motion to suppress the child pornography evidence.

title: Guns Save Life, Inc. v. Ali
description: Whether Cook County's special taxes on the retail purchase of firearms and ammunition violate the uniformity clause of the Illinois Constitution by burdening the fundamental right to bear arms.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the firearm and ammunition taxes violate the Second Amendment, the Illinois Constitution's right to bear arms and uniformity clause, and are preempted by state law, specifically contending that the taxes burden a fundamental right and are not sufficiently related to their stated public safety objective.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the taxes were a proper exercise of Cook County's home rule taxing powers, did not meaningfully impede the right to bear arms, and were substantially related to the important governmental interest of public safety by funding programs to combat gun violence.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the appellate court's judgment, holding that the firearm and ammunition tax ordinances are unconstitutional under the uniformity clause of the Illinois Constitution because they burden a fundamental right without a sufficient relationship between the tax classification and its stated objective.

title: People v. Bochenek
description: Whether the statutory venue provision for identity theft, which allows for proper venue in the county where the victim resides, is constitutional under Article I, Section 8 of the Illinois Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that the venue provision is constitutional because the offense of identity theft can be deemed to have occurred where the victim resides, as the intangible identifying information is 'located' there, and the General Assembly has the authority to define where a crime is committed.
defendant_argument: Bochenek argued that the venue provision is unconstitutional because no aspect of identity theft is connected to the victim's residence, and the offense only occurs where the physical acts were committed.
decision_outcome: The court held that the venue provision for identity theft is constitutional and affirmed the appellate court's judgment, which denied the defendant's motion to dismiss the indictment.

title: People v. Bass
description: Whether a routine traffic stop was unlawfully prolonged by conducting a name check on a passenger, and whether arrests based on investigative alerts violate the Illinois Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the traffic stop was lawfully executed and not unlawfully prolonged, and that investigative alerts are constitutional under both the United States and Illinois Constitutions.
defendant_argument: Bass argued that the traffic stop was unlawfully extended by the name check, violating the Fourth Amendment, and that arrests based on investigative alerts are unconstitutional under the Illinois Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's reversal of Bass's conviction and remand for a new trial, finding the traffic stop was unlawfully prolonged in violation of the Fourth Amendment, and vacated the appellate court's opinion on investigative alerts.
